Japan to Overtake China As World’s Top LNG Importer This Year
Polar LNG's senior executives have…
China’s rare earth dominance leaves…
Charles is a writer for Oilprice.com
Japan is expected to overtake China as the world’s largest importer of liquefied natural gas (LNG) this year, for the first time since 2022, as high LNG prices and sufficient storage in China limit purchases, analysts at ICIS and Kpler say.
Japan’s LNG demand will exceed, albeit slightly, demand in China, according to estimates by the consultancies compiled by Reuters . Imports into Japan are estimated at 62 million metric tons, while Chinese imports are expected at 61 million tons this year, according to ICIS. Kpler also sees a small edge of Japan over China in imports this year, at 63 million tons for Japan compared to 62 million tons for China.
China became the world’s biggest LNG importer in 2021, but the extended Chinese restrictions during two years of COVID-related lockdowns in the country pushed Japan to the top spot again in 2022.
China then regained the top importer status in 2023, and this extended into 2025.
This year, amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis, which halted LNG shipments out of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), overall LNG import demand in Asia has plunged due to the high prices of spot cargoes in a suddenly tight market.
The Chinese decline, however, is set to be more prominent, allowing Japan to overtake China this year.
Chinese LNG buyers acted early to build gas stockpiles amid the Iran war, helping Beijing stock up enough inventories ahead of the winter.
As of the end of September, China’s underground gas storage was 80% full, according to Rystad Energy’s analyst Xiong Wei.
Lower demand for spot supply from China this winter could mean relief for other LNG customers in Asia and Europe, many of which have been struggling with high spot LNG prices and intensified competition for supply that doesn’t need to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
Japan, for its part, this summer reduced gas-fired generation in favor of coal as the price of liquefied natural gas remained elevated. LNG prices surged in Asia to a four-year high as very few cargoes manage to exit the Strait of Hormuz while competition with Europe for winter supply is intensifying.
By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com

articles.title_orig: Exxon, Chevron earnings propelled by war-driven refining surge
articles.title_zh: Exxon, Chevron earnings propelled by war-driven refining surge
articles.content_orig:
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices.
The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. U.S. Gulf Coast refiners have ramped production to help fill the supply gap as diesel prices have surged.
ExxonMobil's profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street's expectations.
"Refining capacity is very tight today," Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. "Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand."
U.S. diesel prices stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA.
Chevron's net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street's expectations of $4.89.
"The system is under stress," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. "We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile."
Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday.
Here's what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon "were making too much money based on a shortage."
Profits from Chevron's refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period.
Chevron's U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said.
Exxon's refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business' earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025.
Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced "record volumes of diesel" in the quarter, Woods said.
Chevron's oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year.
Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025.

articles.title_orig: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
articles.title_zh: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
articles.content_orig:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
articles.title_zh: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds.
Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.
The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data , and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006.
Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury.
Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak , the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset.
As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds . But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say.
"I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates .
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs . President Donald Trump 's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices , economists say.
Consumers expect rising inflation to continue. In September, the one-year inflation outlook jumped to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years, according to a New York Fed survey released in early October.
I bond rates have a variable and fixed rate portion , which the Treasury adjusts every six months, in May and November.
The variable rate is tied to inflation — using the consumer price index percentage change over six months — and stays the same for six months after you purchase, regardless of the Treasury's next update.
Your fixed rate doesn't change after purchasing I bonds. The Treasury doesn't disclose how it calculates fixed-rate adjustments, making it harder to predict.
Some experts believe the I bond fixed rate could be driven by real, or inflation-adjusted, yields from five-year TIPS, according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts.
"There's some uncertainty there," Tumin said.
If you currently own I bonds, rate updates follow a six-month timeline based on your original purchase date.
After you own I bonds for six months, the variable yield changes to the next announced rate. But the fixed rate stays the same for the entire time you own the asset.
For example, let's say you purchased I bonds in March when the variable rate was still 3.12% and the fixed rate was 0.9%. After six months, the variable portion would shift to 3.34%, announced in April 2026 , but your fixed rate would remain 0.9%.
You can earn I bond interest for up to 30 years, or less if you redeem the assets before that. However, you can't cash in I bonds for at least one year after you buy them. If you redeem within five years, you lose your last three months of interest.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq hits near three-month low as Amazon, Intel deepen AI capex concerns
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq hits near three-month low as Amazon, Intel deepen AI capex concerns
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Iain Withers and Ankur Banerjee
LONDON/SINGAPORE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Tech shares slumped on Friday and US bonds surged toward their biggest monthly gain in nearly three years, as investors scurried to safety due to worries that huge and rising AI spending may not deliver sufficient returns.
Futures trading pointed to ‌falls on Wall Street later in the session, including a more than 2.5% drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100. That came alongside an out-of-hours plunge ‌of 25% in Intel shares and a drop of 6% in Amazon as their results showed they burned through cash.
Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell 12.6% on Wall Street on Thursday and slid a little further after hours, ​to wipe out a stunning $500 billion in market value, as massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative.
European stocks were last down 0.3% on Friday, as the relative lack of big tech stocks helped limit losses. There were falls earlier in Asia led by chipmakers.
Investors are worried about the returns they can expect to make on the massive capital spending needed for the AI buildout and what effect it could have on consumers if price hikes squeeze global demand for devices like smartphones and PCs. Anthropic's potentially record-breaking IPO could prove the ‌next big test of sentiment.
"The next key milestone will be ⁠the Anthropic IPO, to see how that lands. If it's a poor listing, I think that could signal a bit of weakness going forward," said Jason Da Silva, co-chief investment officer at Arbuthnot Latham.
Nerves were also frayed by a potentially record-breaking hack at Binance, the ⁠world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, which drove down bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency, bitcoin, hit a six-week low before cutting losses to trade 1.7% lower at $77,471.
"I suspect the negative price action still has some way to go," said Geoffrey Kendrick, head of digital assets research at Standard Chartered. "Only after assets are unfrozen and more detail of the hack emerges will we find ​a ​new base."
In commodities, oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday and were poised for a ​fourth monthly gain, as an attack on a tanker in the ‌Strait of Hormuz waterway highlighted continuing supply risks from the US-Israeli war on Iran. [O/R]
Gold prices fell to their lowest since mid-July and were last at $3,970, headed for a second straight monthly decline, as rising crude oil prices and persistent inflation worries reinforced expectations of US interest rate hikes.
The Bank of Japan left interest rates on hold, which was expected and did not trigger major currency or bond moves, although in a surprise development the central bank unveiled plans to sharply accelerate exchange-traded fund sales next year.
"While this may initially spook markets, I actually think this is a positive development since the BOJ feels confident enough with the economy and market," said David Chao, global market ‌strategist for Asia-Pacific at Invesco.
The central bank declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit ​its price target and signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could come as ​soon as December.
Tech sector jitters have helped push a rush to bonds, further ​spurred by the Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday to keep US interest rates on hold, with no firm projection of when it ‌might hike next.
Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell around 8 basis points ​on Friday to 4.91% and were on ​track for their largest one-month drop since December 2023. Yields fall when bond prices rise.
The risk-averse mood strengthened haven currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc, with the yen slightly higher at 157.05 per dollar and the franc at 0.821 to the dollar and not far from a one-month high.
The euro inched ​up 0.1% to $1.1193 but was set for a drop of ‌over 1% in October, its second straight monthly decline.
The euro zone economy grew faster than predicted last quarter, data showed, with the economies of ​the 21 nations sharing the euro growing by 0.4% in the third quarter.
(Reporting by Iain Withers in London and Tom Westbrook and Ankur Banerjee in ​Singapore; Editing by Tom Hogue, Clarence Fernandez, Stephen Coates, William Maclean and Chizu Nomiyama )

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 is here, and alongside new features for Apple Photos , Messages , and Siri AI , the update also has a welcome addition for Find My: support for Apple TV 4K remotes.
Find My has long been the iPhone’s go-to hub for locating people as well as your Apple devices.
Except until now, there’s been one Apple device not included in the app.
The Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K has historically been absent from Find My. There was another way to locate it using the Remote app via Control Center, but most users probably didn’t realize that feature existed.
But with iOS 27.2, Apple TV remotes have now been added to the Find My app for location tracking. Open Find My in iOS 27.2 and go to the Devices tab, and compatible Siri Remotes (2nd gen and later) will now appear there.
It’s nice that Apple finally addressed this oversight, but the timing is no coincidence. That’s because the new Siri Remote (4th gen) is going to make finding a lost remote way easier.
The new remote features Precision Finding support and a built-in speaker . So the next time it’s lost somewhere in your house, your iPhone can direct you step-by-step to its location and trigger a noise to help.
The new Siri Remote is included with the 4th generation Apple TV 4K. But you can also buy it separately for $59 and get the same new features.
The upgraded remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models. To benefit from Precision Finding though, you’ll need an iPhone 17 or newer.
Did you know the Remote app offered support for finding a lost remote? Will you use the new feature in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
articles.title_zh: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Some 69 people have been confirmed dead but the toll may rise further, with at least 70 people reported missing
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s deadly train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.
Sánchez said the Spanish state was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding that his government was committed to finding what had caused Spain’s second deadly train collision this year.
Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am . After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear , knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
“ It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.
“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system.
Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken ; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”
Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente – who is under growing pressure to resign – gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.
“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “ The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”
Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but stressed that such incidents were not at all uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers ultimately reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.
Bulgaria’s next president will be elected in a runoff vote on Sunday, after a close race between the two main contenders ended inconclusively in the first round.
The incumbent Iliana Yotova , former vice-president to Bulgaria’s former president and current prime minister Rumen Radev , faces pro-European opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov.
The two candidates will pit contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarised contest on Sunday, AP noted.
Contrary to pre-election expectations by observers for a double-digit difference in favour of Yotova, her opponent showed a surprisingly strong performance coming just 2.8 percentage points behind her and leaving all options open for the runoff.
AP noted that Bulgarians vote against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping, which have left several sailors dead or missing.
Polls will open 7am local time and close 8pm local time.
The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it is closing, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” the editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said in a video statement published on YouTube on Friday. “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile. Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed by Moscow as a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Sokolov said: “ Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On 9 November we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
This month Sokolov was taken in for questioning and Russian authorities searched his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Russia has intensified its crackdown on independent news outlets since its offensive on Ukraine in February 2022. Novaya Gazeta cut down production inside Russia after the offensive began. Authorities revoked its media licence the same year.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.
In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”.
With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.
Student List candidate Svetlana Stanarević was applauded when she accused the officials of violating the law. She also called for the director of Serbia’s internal intelligence agency to resign, accusing him of running the organisation as “a party security service, not a state security service”.
There was approval, too, for the “reopening or expediting of cases” related to the disaster that sparked the student protest movement. Sunday will mark the second anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. There have yet to be any convictions.
The announcements on Thursday were the Student List’s way of stressing they intended to put anti-corruption efforts at the heart of government.
“For years, for decades, people have been really frustrated,” said Iva Marković, a Student List candidate and political ecologist who founded the Right to Water initiative.
“We see this as a time where everyone who was honestly and credibly working within [public] institutions can do their jobs. They are no longer under political pressure, and we ask them to do their jobs, which also means for prosecutors to prosecute, and police to investigate.”
Having spent days bathing in the euphoria of their unexpected triumph , the candidates’ focus was now clear: the cleaning up of the rotten institutions that had increasingly blighted the lives of Serbs over the 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS). They called for the dismissal of many senior law enforcement officials, among them the chiefs of the criminal police, the paramilitary gendarmerie and an anti-terrorism unit.
Reinforcing the student movement’s key principles is also a way, perhaps, to allay concerns that the Student List might not know how to handle its stunning victory over Vučić and the SNS .

articles.title_orig: Why Electronic Arts Shut Down BioWare And Cancelled ‘Mass Effect’
articles.title_zh: Why Electronic Arts Shut Down BioWare And Cancelled ‘Mass Effect’
articles.content_orig:
In his first interview since BioWare’s closure, Greg Zeschuk discusses EA’s acquisition, the leveraged buyout he calls the “final nail in the coffin,” and why great studios cannot be rebuilt with “random people and AI.”
BREAKING: BioWare Is Shutting Down
Greg Zeschuk was standing in the Babine River deep in northern British Columbia, fishing for steelhead when the studio died.
He didn’t find out until later that Wednesday, returning to the lodge, its sporadic cell connection, and a flurry of text messages.
BioWare, a studio he co-founded with Ray Muzyka and Augustine Yip in 1995 , which arguably went on to redefine the role-playing video game genre, launched some of the most respected games over its three decades, and helped earn Zeschuk and Muzyka the Order of Canada , was shuttered.
EA announced Oct. 21 that it was closing BioWare and ending early development on the next Mass Effect game . The closure cost about 50 jobs at the studio, part of roughly 400 layoffs across EA, and came 78 days after the company’s $55 billion buyout closed.
“I got like ten texts,” he said. “I came off the river and got to my little room and opened my phone, and it’s like, ‘I’m so sorry to hear about BioWare.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh sh*t.’”
He said by the time he flew home that Friday, he had “already shelved it away.” He also spoke with Muzyka, who declined, through Zeschuk, to speak with me for this story. Zeschuk said he turned down other interview requests while he was away; this is his first interview about the closure.
“I didn't have the immediate impact,” Zeschuk said, speaking with me from his home in Edmonton, where BioWare was also based, this week. “I wasn't there to share in the moment, which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it.”
“I’m not saying it doesn’t hurt and doesn’t suck. And I think it’s kind of sad. It’s actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we’re from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that.”
In a way Zeschuk already grieved the loss of BioWare 14 years ago when he and Muzyka both retired from the gaming industry in the same month.
“I've kind of gone through all the emotions like long, long ago,” he said. Leaving a company in a healthy way, he added, means breaking that emotional attachment. “You have to break from it and kind of go, ‘OK, I've had my emotional moment.’”
The real sadness with this news came from his concern about the people involved who lost their jobs and knowing how tough the games business is, he said.
“Anyone getting put into the job hunt is a sort of terrifying endeavor and super sad,” he said.
Some might believe that the writing was on the wall for BioWare when the founders sold the studio to Electronic Arts in 2007, but that’s not Zeschuk’s take.
In 2013, I chatted with Zeschuk about his decision to leave the company and pursue his love of craft beer. At the time, he talked about surviving EA.
“I think one of the reasons that we survived and succeeded within EA was that our company was mature enough and there was enough good people throughout to handle the EA bear hug – something that is well-meaning but vigorous,” he said at the time. “We needed to be strong to survive that, and I think we did, and you evolve from that as well."
This week, I brought up that bear hug again. Did BioWare ultimately succumb to it, I asked. Zeschuk said EA gave the studio several shots after he left, with Dragon Age: The Veilguard the last.
“They were able to operate within the framework, and they were able to put out products, I think,” he said. “And so that for me seems like it's a success.”
The first three shots happened, he said, “which is, I think, a pretty huge success.” The fourth, the next Mass Effect, never got its chance after the buyout.
He added that he doesn’t regret selling to EA, and he rejected the idea that BioWare sold because it was in trouble. “There was no coercion or pressure,” he said. “We were in good shape.”
“A lot of it had to do with the funding of the Star Wars project in Austin and just the stability of being in a bigger company,” he said. “I think at the end of the day, maybe we were ahead of the game a bit, but like we saw there'd be value in being part of something bigger rather than going our own way and taking all the risks.
“We had options actually. We thought we chose the best option that was available to us at the time. The company had good possibilities going forward, but at the end of the day we felt, OK, we may be better as part of a bigger thing.”
Zeschuk, like many founders in the game industry that I’ve interviewed, took a bit of a break from gaming when he first retired from the game industry. But these days, he says he loves playing games.
That said, he hasn’t played everything BioWare created since his departure.
“I played a bit of Anthem, but I didn’t play Andromeda,” he said. “I had a cooling-off period for a couple of years. Then I got back into it, and I’m a pretty avid player now.” As he’s gotten older, he said, he’s transitioned a bit away from story-driven games and more into what he calls “aggression-based” games. For instance, he said he’s played a ton of Nioh, Nioh 2, and Nioh 3, and enthused about completing the Underworld endgame mode in Nioh 2.
“I think I have over 1,200 hours in that,” he said. “I really like combat games. Maybe that’s where Jade Empire came from.”
He’s also a huge fan of Elden Ring, which he called probably the greatest game ever made. “Though the Zeldas are pretty close.”
I asked him if there’s a moment in time when he can look at BioWare and say that’s when the studio stopped being the thing that he and the other founders created. But he said a change like that at a studio is more of an evolution than a sudden switch.
“The way I look at that kind of stuff is studios are a function of the people, right?” he said. “As the people start leaving, it starts evolving and different people come in. I'm not going to have so much hubris to say Ray and I were the linchpin in the chain, our departure ruined everything. It wasn't that at all. I think we had a strong team with lots of people and there's lots of backup for things we brought and back up to the backup. But just over time, there's an evolution.”
He added that BioWare was always a very entrepreneurial kind of company, but that doesn’t really fit inside a bigger company.
“So I think it’s a slow and insidious kind of thing and again it’s the people. The people are the key.”
Zeschuk said that when he heard that EA was purchased in a $55 billion leveraged buyout led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in August, he had an inkling things wouldn’t end well for BioWare.
“I think it was the final nail in the coffin,” he said. “I think that was the crux of it in a sense. Once again it's a completely different company now.”
And as a completely different company the new EA has a new set of priorities. While Zeschuk doesn’t have any inside knowledge, his suspicion is that the purchase was mostly about sports titles and “maybe Battlefield.”
“Everything else is kind of extraneous I suspect,” he said. “BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways.”
Not everyone who reacted to the closure of BioWare has been as measured. Warren Spector, the now-retired designer behind Deus Ex and System Shock, called the closure “utter bulls**t” in a LinkedIn post , and said the executives involved should lose their jobs instead of the developers.
Zeschuk said he can understand that reaction. “Honestly, it’s not my rodeo,” he said. “I had to break with it emotionally 15 years ago…It’s so much healthier just to really, truly create that emotional break. Or else you’ll forever be second-guessing it a

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and foreign dignitaries will descend on Atlanta this week for two days of meetings focused on economic and security challenges.
The event, spanning Friday and Saturday, will feature the Group of 20, an international forum composed of leaders from more than a dozen countries along with the African and European Unions.
It is the latest in a series of high-profile gatherings of foreign officials in the U.S., as the country currently holds the forum’s rotating presidency. The group’s finance, trade, energy and other ministers have already met. The culminating event is the G20 Leaders Summit in mid-December in Miami.

articles.title_zh: Xi tells German president China and EU must ‘stay anchored to their partnership’
articles.content_orig:
Frank-Walter Steinmeier was visiting Beijing at a time of heightened concern in Brussels over the widening trade gap
China and the European Union can resolve their differences through dialogue, Chinese President Xi Jinping told his German counterpart Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Friday.
“China has always regarded the European Union as a partner,” Xi said, according to state broadcaster CCTV, adding that cooperation between the two sides outweighed competition.
“As long as [both sides] stay anchored to their partnership and engage in dialogue on an equal footing, differences and challenges can always be resolved and will not stand in the way of China-EU relations moving forward,” the Chinese leader said.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Cancels Kirby Air Riders Halloween Event Following Performance Woes
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Cancels Kirby Air Riders Halloween Event Following Performance Woes
articles.content_orig:
If you have been keeping up with Kirby Air Riders of late, you might have been excited to dive into the game's new Halloween event this weekend and pick up some spooky Ghost headwear while you're at it. Well, we're sorry, but that's not going to happen, as Nintendo has cancelled the event.
The event was originally scheduled to run from 28th October through until 4th November, but many players reported nasty technical difficulties when taking part in early matches, where the screen would regularly freeze — which, in a game as frantic as Air Riders, isn't going to cut it.
You can see the issue for yourself below (shared on Bluesky by TAHK0 ):
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 854k
This time, Nintendo didn't have a quick fix up its sleeve, so it decided to cancel the event instead. "We have confirmed an issue in the currently ongoing event 'Trick or Treat!' where the screen temporarily freezes during gameplay," a message from the Japanese Nintendo Support social media account (via machine translation) read this morning. "For this reason, we will be cancelling this event."
While Nintendo went on to apologise for the cancellation, it claimed that there are plans to hold the event again in the future, so everyone can get in on the themed reward. There's no official news on when it will return at the moment, but we have to imagine it will be sooner rather than later.

articles.title_orig: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.title_zh: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent the week punishing Big Tech's biggest AI spenders . Amazon ( AMZN ) just posted the deepest cash burn in its history.
Amazon's free cash flow — the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses, and equipment — was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September, according to its third quarter results released Thursday. That's nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.
One quarter did most of the damage. Amazon spent about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
So far, the spending is working.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) grew 39% to about $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon's operating margin of nearly 14% was its highest ever. CEO Andy Jassy said in the release that he projects AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) computing commitments alone amount to about a fifth of AWS's backlog as of June , according to Yahoo Finance calculations based on the AI lab's IPO filing.
Paying for it has meant borrowing. Amazon's long-term debt reached about $173 billion at the end of September, up from about $66 billion at the end of 2025, while its cash fell to about $56 billion from about $87 billion. Meta ( META ) took a different route this week with a nearly $100 billion stock sale .
Bond traders have noticed. The cost of insuring Amazon's debt against default for five years with credit default swaps has risen about 50% since early August, according to Bloomberg data. That price implies roughly a 7% chance of default over five years, up from about 5%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Amazon stock fell about 4% Thursday to its lowest close since July 30 as Alphabet's record drop weighed on Big Tech. It slid further after-hours as sales, earnings, and its profit outlook for the holiday quarter missed estimates.
Amazon isn't planning to ease off. CEO Andy Jassy said on the company's earnings call Thursday that Amazon still expects to spend about $220 billion this year, mostly on AWS, and to "spend meaningfully more in 2027."
"Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that's not the world that we live in," Jassy said. "We can fund this plan. I think it will forever change the size of Amazon."

articles.title_orig: 'Bad time to troll': Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao asks Elon Musk for 'respect' after post about bitcoin hack
articles.title_zh: 'Bad time to troll': Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao asks Elon Musk for 'respect' after post about bitcoin hack
articles.content_orig:
The cofounder and former CEO of Binance asked Elon Musk not to "troll" the company on Friday and instead "show some support" after the SpaceX CEO appeared to mock the embattled cryptocurrency exchange in a series of social media posts.
After learning the world's largest crypto exchange had been hit by a $6.3 billion hack late Thursday, Musk posted several emojis, ranging from laughing to grimacing, on X.
In response, Changpeng Zhao reminded the SpaceX and Tesla CEO of Binance's equity stake in Musk's businesses.
Binance’s SpaceX stake, which stems from an earlier investment in what was then-Twitter, is worth more than $1 billion, Zhao said.
That's a tiny fraction of SpaceX's roughly $2 trillion valuation.
"Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop," Zhao wrote. "Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!"
It's not the first time the pair has sparred online.
In Nov. 2021, Binance suspended Dogecoin withdrawals because of a wallet glitch, a measure Musk called "shady". In reply, Zhao highlighted a major Tesla recall of almost 12,000 U.S. vehicles due to software glitches and hardware issues.
Binance froze all withdrawals and deposits after the hack, which investigators suspect to be the work of North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor. It has since restored deposits.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu's party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu's party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
articles.content_orig:
JERUSALEM — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.
Results released by election officials early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.
Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "serious suspicions" of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!" it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was "aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government."
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous."
As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been "entirely unfounded."
"It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said.
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. "They are doing this because they lost," he said.
Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: "I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel."
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner."
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless."
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc's candidate.
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.

articles.title_orig: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
articles.title_zh: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
articles.content_orig:
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

articles.title_orig: Police Investigate Former Prince Andrew and Epstein’s Time at Balmoral, Royal Estate in Scotland
articles.title_zh: Police Investigate Former Prince Andrew and Epstein’s Time at Balmoral, Royal Estate in Scotland
articles.content_orig:
Force says it has received ‘information’ on pair’s stay at royal estate as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor
Detectives in Scotland are investigating Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s stay at Balmoral castle as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor amid allegations that women were trafficked to the royal estate.
Police Scotland said it had received “information” and inquiries were at a “very early stage” into the time the disgraced royal spent with the child sex offender at Balmoral.
The late Epstein, who was convicted in 2008 of soliciting sex from girls, and Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking a minor, stayed at Balmoral in 1999.
Pictures previously released by the US Department of Justice appear to show Andrew and Epstein shooting on the estate.
The Daily Express has reported that the inquiries relate to claims that women were trafficked to the estate.
A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing, but these are at a very early stage. All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries. We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”
Other investigations linked to the release of the Epstein files were ongoing within several forces, including Thames Valley police, the Metropolitan police and Surrey police, the National Police Chiefs’ Council confirmed.
An NPCC spokesperson said: “Identifying any further potential offending, suspects, victims or witnesses is a complex process and will take time, but UK policing remains committed to carrying out a meticulous assessment of the material released by the US Department of Justice.”
There was no national investigation at present, the NPCC said.
The former Duke of York was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office on 19 February this year, his 66th birthday, after allegations he had shared sensitive information with Epstein during his time as a UK trade envoy. He was interviewed under caution before being released under investigation. He denies wrongdoing, with the police investigation continuing.
An email released in a tranche of the Epstein files last year and signed by “A” asked the disgraced British socialite Maxwell for “inappropriate friends”. In one of four emails sent to Maxwell in August 2001 by someone using the name the Invisible Man, the sender told her their “valet” had recently died and they had “left the RN”.
Mountbatten-Windsor left the Royal Navy the month before the email was sent. Another email from the same individual, dated 16 August 2001, said they were at “Balmoral summer camp for the royal family” before asking Maxwell: “Have you found me some inappropriate friends?”
In March 2002, an email from Maxwell to the Invisible Man said she had passed on a message to an unnamed individual, with that message beginning: “I just gave Andrew your telephone no.”
The message from Maxwell to the unidentified person also said “Andrew” would be “very happy” if he did some “two legged sight seeing”.
Andrew was the UK’s special representative for international trade and investment from 2001-11, when he stepped down amid controversy over his friendship with Epstein.
He received no salary for travelling around the world and the UK promoting Britain’s business interests, but criticisms were made about the thousands of pounds spent each year on his expenses and travel costs.
His decision to quit the role came in the same year he was pictured with his arm around his primary accuser, Virginia Giuffre, who said she had been trafficked to the former duke at the home of Maxwell.
Andrew paid Giuffre, a woman he has claimed never to have met, millions of pounds to settle a civil suit in the US in 2022.
Giuffre died by suicide, aged 41, in April 2025.

articles.title_orig: Alphabet stock crash leaves this trading metric at a level not seen in more than a decade
articles.title_zh: Alphabet stock crash leaves this trading metric at a level not seen in more than a decade
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Investing in the future of internet search and YouTube has rarely been this cheap.
Shares of Alphabet ( GOOGL ) are trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio not seen since 2012, Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data shows (chart below).
The metric comes in the wake of Alphabet shares plunging a stunning 12.6% on Thursday after the earnings report, wiping out nearly $500 billion in market value. Shares lost another 1% in premarket trading on Friday.
The sell-off was warranted, despite Google delivering strong third quarter growth for a company its size.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate of negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), this is not the number the Street wanted to see.
"Alphabet's 3Q results and the stock's sharp move lower show us the margin for error when a hyperscaler spending hundreds of billions on the AI infrastructure buildout and flipping to negative FCF posts disappointing results in the core," JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth wrote in a note. "Not that there was much debate going in—most investors seemed to understand that strong Google Cloud growth, including early TPU ramp, wouldn't be enough to offset a Search shortfall, which was telegraphed in third-party data."
13 Wall Street analysts cut their price target on Alphabet in the aftermath.

articles.title_orig: Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
articles.title_zh: Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
articles.content_orig:
A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.
Andreas Malm told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had received a letter from the Home Office notifying him that his presence was "not conducive to the public good", with no further details given.
He said he could not "see any other explanation" for being denied entry than his scheduled appearance with Huda Ammori, a founder of the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.
The Home Office said it did not comment on individual cases.
Malm is a senior lecturer in human ecology at Sweden's Lund University, whose work includes the 2021 book How to Blow up a Pipeline and 2025's The Destruction of Palestine is the Destruction of the Earth.
He said he had asked the Home Office to explain its decision, but could not see a reason beyond the upcoming talk in London with Ammori organised by the left-wing magazine Tribune - calling the move a "severe restriction on the free exchange of ideas".
Malm said he was not a member of Palestine Action, had never publicly endorsed it, nor had he given it any financial support.
"The only link to Palestine Action is her as a person," he said, criticising the UK government for ascribing "guilt by association".
The academic acknowledged that he had previously described the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel - in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage - as "fundamentally an act of liberation".
Malm said it was possible that these remarks, during a December 2023 talk in which he also condemned the "deplorable" killing of civilians in the cross-border attack, had been the reason for the Home Office's decision.
But he argued that these views had been in the public realm for a long time, including when he was last allowed into the UK to deliver a talk in May.
"I don't expect the British state to agree with me on Palestine or climate or anything. What I expect the British state to do is to continue to let me enter the country and to discuss with colleagues, with people who disagree with me - as I have done for years."
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's controversial ban under terrorism legislation . The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of the group. About 2,500 have been charged, though none have gone to trial as the legal challenge to the proscription continues.
The government has broad discretion to bar foreign nationals from entering the UK if their presence is deemed to pose a risk to society.
In April, 11 people described by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer as "far-right agitators" were banned from entering the UK ahead of a rally led by Tommy Robinson.
Kanye West was also denied entry that same month after backlash to his planned set at London's Wireless Festival, following a string of antisemitic, racist and pro-Nazi comments. He had previously apologised for the remarks and said his bipolar disorder had caused him to lose "touch with reality".
Left-wing political commentators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur claimed in June that their visas had been revoked ahead of planned appearances in London and Oxford, allegedly "for criticising Israel" .

articles.title_orig: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
articles.title_zh: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
articles.content_orig:
My ears perked up when I heard Apple’s new foldable phones were cracking . I licked my lips when the company announced it’s releasing a touch-screen laptop . This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth , asked $200 for a VESA mount , and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it’s borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected.
The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO — a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard.
With Ternus at the helm, I feel there’s a good chance Apple’s best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it’s déclassé. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It’s in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to “Think Different” is now releasing hardware that’s just like everything else on the market.
Apple is not adjusting to this new position well. AI boosters agree that Siri AI is awful. Apple HomeView is a $300 Apple Watch meant to replace the family hearth . The iPhone Duo has only been out for a few days and all people can talk about is the cracks, yet Ternus is on the cover of Time Magazine this week holding the folding iPhone Duo and staring at the camera. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus told Time . Many people holding cracked iPhone Duos this week are learning just what (not) cheap and crappy looks like.
Flailing from crackgate, Apple announced the launch of a touch-screen laptop, an idea Steve Jobs extensively tested and said “doesn’t work ,” an idea Cook once compared to combining a toaster with a refrigerator . What’s next? What if the toaster-refigerator folded? Ternus has been trying to make an 18-inch foldable iPad happen for years . Maybe Apple will solve the screen cracking issues by then. Or maybe Ternus will continue to try to put a hat on a hat .
I have been waiting for this moment for more than a decade. I am relishing Apple’s recent trajectory more than I should. I confess I harbor a secret and petty grudge.
In 2010, when Apple released the iPhone 4 I was working as a floor manager at a Banana Republic in Dallas. I was interested in smart phones, of course, but Dallas is an expensive city and the iPhone was a luxury. I made do with my Motorola Razr . But the suit-wearing middle management retail psychopaths that were my coworkers saw my lack of an iPhone as a weakness. It was not, as they say now, On Brand.
I had started at the store in the stock room, working my way up to manage the backroom before ascending to a coveted position on the sales floor. The other managers made it clear that a Razr was a “backroom” phone and someone in a prominent position on the floor needed to be seen using an iPhone.
At first, I was not told to buy an iPhone. The message came in the form of subtle and not so subtle bullying deployed over weeks.
“Still using that old phone?” they’d say.“Didn’t you get a raise?” someone would ask a week later.
“Try not to use that thing on the sales floor,” one co-worker told me, pointing at my Razr. “We’re trying to project a certain image here.”
The social pressure had the opposite of its intended effect. I resisted. Eventually one of the friendlier managers pulled me aside. He told me that my colleagues thought it was weird that I didn't have an iPhone. He said I needed to buy one to fit in and he said the store could give me an advance on my paycheck to make it happen.
Ever the contrarian and pissed I was experiencing high school style bullying as a full grown adult, I threw in with Google instead. I got an HTC Dream . My coworkers weren’t happy, but they stopped bringing up the iPhone.
I’ve been an Android user ever since and studiously avoided Apple products until I broke down a few years ago and bought a Macbook Air. Time heals all wounds and Windows laptops are garbage. I’d even been considering changing from Android to iPhone because the privacy features are more robust. I’ve never been averse to a fast food meal either and maybe I’m a little more comfortable with Apple now that the cracks are starting to show in the foldable phone.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Trump says war "going to end soon" as Qatar pushes for a U.S.-Iran deal
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Trump says war "going to end soon" as Qatar pushes for a U.S.-Iran deal
articles.content_orig:
Major U.S. oil and gas giant ExxonMobil reported Friday that its third-quarter profits had more than doubled to $15.4 billion, as it benefited from higher oil prices and refining margins due to the U.S.-Iran war.
Profits in the period were slightly more than double the $7.5 billion in the year-ago period.
Oil prices have been high since the start of the war. As of Friday, the two main benchmark products, Brent crude and U.S. West Texas Intermediate, remained up about 70% compared to a year ago.
The Iranian navy said Friday that an enemy drone was "struck and destroyed" east of the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the navy also said two oil tankers "were damaged and caught fire after striking naval mines," accusing the vessels of ignoring warnings and navigating in prohibited and unsafe waters with their tracking systems switched off.
It was not immediately clear if the two vessels referred to by the Iranian navy were the same tankers that Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps reported earlier Friday to have hit mines in the strait.
President ⁠Donald Trump said Friday that the war with Iran is "going to get wrapped up soon."
Speaking to Kansas ‌City radio station KCMO ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the president said "it's going to get wrapped ⁠up soon," without specifying how.
"We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon," he added.
The commander of the U.S. military's Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, reiterated his longstanding assertions on Friday that Iran's navy is "at the bottom of the sea" and that southern commercial shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz are clear of Iranian mines and safe to navigate.
In a video posted on social media , Cooper said the U.S. had helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer, while the U.S. naval blockade had prevented Iran from exporting any oil through the strait.
Cooper said he had recently flown over the strait and seen U.S. military "assets in the air and on the water."
"What I didn't see," said Cooper, was Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps "out there at all. They patrolled the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters for decades, harassing and threatening and seizing commercial vessels at will, but they were not out there because Iran's navy is all at the bottom of the sea."
Cooper renewed the claim made by President Trump and the Pentagon since late August that "we also successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognized primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines. And today, U.S. forces remain highly vigilant and present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."
His comments came a day after Iran's navy claimed four vessels had struck sea mines and been disabled as the attempted to transit the strait via the U.S.-backed southern route. The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening, meanwhile, that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the strait.
It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines.
A source familiar with the ongoing diplomacy confirmed to CBS News that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday to convey the latest edits to a draft proposal to end the U.S. war with Iran.
The source said there were indications of progress being made.
A draft was presented by Qatari mediators last Sunday, and a response from Iran is expected by the weekend. The aim of the proposal is to avert a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which President Trump has threatened multiple times in recent weeks.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that two oil tankers had been halted after unspecified "incidents" as they attempted to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has repeatedly warned shippers that using the southern route through the waterway, which has been promoted by the U.S., puts them at risk as the regime deems it an illegal passage.
The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist U.S. military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route," the IRGC statement said.
The IRGC did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had been forced to stop in the area after hitting sea mines.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Qatari officials returned to Iran on Friday to push for a peace deal between Tehran and Washington, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency , along with Reuters and AFP, reported.
The talks have been coordinated with the U.S., an official told Reuters.
The delegation is led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister and is scheduled to meet with senior Iranian officials, IRNA said, adding that the discussions would focus on bilateral relations between Iran and Qatar, as well as developments in the region.
An official briefed on the latest diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , and that Tehran would not change its stance on the nuclear issue, something Washington wants included in negotiations from the start.
Tehran wants the U.S. to first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to drop sanctions limiting the country's gas and oil sales.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by President Trump but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
On Thursday, Mr. Trump said a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei — which was reported by multiple outlets as an attempt to restart peace negotiations — was an outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran has yet to reply to the letter, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.
Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.
Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.
The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations , which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it stopped using the name Operation Epic Fury for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
