articles.title_orig: The Apple Pencil turned the Duo into my new favorite notebook
articles.title_zh: The Apple Pencil turned the Duo into my new favorite notebook
articles.content_orig:
Ignore the pile of previous favorite notebooks; this is the one that’s gonna change it all for me.
Ignore the pile of previous favorite notebooks; this is the one that’s gonna change it all for me.
Apple’s $2,000 folding phone is a surprisingly good stand-in for a $20 notebook.
Believe me; nothing gets me going quite like a new notebook. This one will be different, I think. This time, I really will take it everywhere. Inspiration can strike at any moment, and you have to be ready, says David Sedaris in that one MasterClass I watched on a flight. With this one special new notebook, I will see the world differently. I’ll steal moments for myself to write, rather than pulling out my phone to scroll at every opportunity like a trained monkey. And a few weeks, a month, or maybe a year later, I’ll concede that it didn’t change everything and add it to my notebook graveyard. At least they all look nice on the corner of my desk?
The iPhone Duo is not a notebook — although it is the first iPhone to support the Apple Pencil. Even so, I can see the new notebook effect in the eyes of the people I talk to about the Duo. “Is that the new iPhone?” the conversation starts. I hand over the phone and give them the short version of our 26-minute review : It’s nice, it’s kind of heavy and chunky, you should wait for the second generation. They nod, but I can tell they still want one anyway. They’re tired of their big/aging/boring phone, they tell me. And this one would be different.
It’s hard to argue against. It really is a different phone. Its new form factor lets you actually use it in meaningfully different ways. The Duo can act like a vintage Hasselblad with a waist-level viewfinder. It can be a book-shaped e-reader. And with this week’s iOS 27.2 update officially adding that Apple Pencil support, it can also be a notebook.
Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something.
That’s the USB-C Apple Pencil, to be specific, so there’s no pressure sensitivity. You do still get the ability to “scribble” handwriting that’s automatically turned into text in apps like Messages or Safari, as you can on the iPad. But even with the basic stylus, there’s a lot of fun to be had doodling and writing notes out by hand. I asked for some Pencil-friendly app suggestions and downloaded a handful. I used the native Notes app to scribble down some article ideas. I set my five-year-old loose on a blank note, to his delight (the phone survived the encounter, too). But having the stylus in my hand led me on an unexpected side quest: turning the whole phone into a notebook.
Why not? It’s notebook-shaped. Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something. Maybe I could cajole the Duo into being something less distracting, more input-friendly. I put together a minimalist home and lockscreen designed around this theory. I won’t lie, it’s pretty nice. But I don’t think I curated my way out of the new-notebook trap, even if it was a fun exercise.
There aren’t many apps ready to take advantage of the new stylus support. Notes, unsurprisingly, is where the Pencil is at its best. When you use the Pencil for handwriting in the app, you can enable the auto-refine handwriting feature that neatens up your writing while still keeping its unique characteristics intact. This has been available on the iPad since 2024 , and it’s particularly useful on the Duo’s comparatively small screens.
It occasionally gets tripped up by some of my scrawl that it either doesn’t know what to do with or misinterprets — it kept insisting on turning a “u” into an “o” in one instance. And it works after a small delay when you pause your writing, which I can see being distracting if I really want to get into a flow state. But it’s a nice middle ground between my untidy scribbles and full handwriting-to-text conversion and very handy for something like a grocery list.
The Notes app also has a big homescreen widget that kind of turned the phone into a notebook, but wasn’t nice to look at. After some more digging , I found almost exactly what I’d been looking for: TypeDraw .
It’s a $4.99 one-time purchase, and it’s optimized for the Duo. When you launch the app, it turns the cover screen into the front of your notebook. To flip to a page, you can either swipe on the cover screen or open the whole phone. It’s a delight.
TypeDraw isn’t really for power note-takers the way other apps like Bear are . You can’t add tags or links between notes, and you’re limited to one notebook. But it automatically creates a table of contents at the beginning based on the headings of your notes, so you can skip right to the section you’re looking for. Plus, if you drag your finger along the “elastic” on the cover, it’ll stretch and snap back, complete with satisfying haptics. I have zero regrets about the five bucks I spent on this app.
Using the Apple Pencil with the Duo gave me one more reason to love the matte finish on the inner screen. There’s just a bit of resistance moving the pencil across the display that feels more satisfying than the lifeless plastic-on-glass effect of writing on the cover screen. It’s not going to feel like using a Remarkable tablet or anything, but it’s nice.
The Pencil has one other neat trick — it can stick to the Duo’s hinge magnetically when the phone is closed. The pencil is longer than the phone, so it’s an awkward fit, but it’s been a handy way to carry both around the house as I relocate throughout the day.
I was only, like, 60 percent serious when I set out to turn the Duo into a notebook, but I actually liked the idea the more I got into it. Reimagining my homescreen around creating rather than consuming feels like a worthwhile cause, and I’m planning to live with it for a while to see if it inspires any changes in my phone habits. To that end, I also set up a shortcut to launch TypeDraw whenever I open the inner screen.
But I think the most useful part of this exercise was examining, once again, how much stuff I really need on my homescreen. I can get most things done with a Spotlight Search or a tap in the Control Center. Siri is much more helpful now too, and it’s always lurking nearby to help out. The grid of apps I’m so used to is mostly for emotional support at this point. I didn’t need a folding phone to learn that, but it helped.
Above all, the new-notebook effect proved to be just as strong as always. The shiny new thing eventually fades into the background. You certainly don’t need a $2,000 phone to reevaluate your homescreen. You can — and I will continue to — just carry a little notebook around with your regular phone. A fun new gadget is delightful, don’t get me wrong. But don’t hang all your hopes and dreams for a new you on one of them.

articles.title_orig: The big questions remaining after Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO prospectus
articles.title_zh: The big questions remaining after Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO prospectus
articles.content_orig:
This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.
Anthropic's over 300 page S-1 filing earlier this week contained a lot of information. It was the most comprehensive public statement to date about how a pure-play AI lab makes its money.
After the prospectus went live on Monday, my U.S.-based colleagues and I went through it with a fine-tooth comb , detailing everything from revenue and risks to competitors and computing costs.
The filing also revealed that CEO Dario Amodei and his six co-founders each own over 200 million shares, which could be worth billions if Anthropic hits the over $1 trillion valuation it's expected to.
But despite all the nuggets, a few big questions remain.
Anthropic reported its cost of revenue as $2.38 billion in the first half of 2026, booking $16.29 billion in revenue during the same period and implying a gross margin of 85%.
Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares, told CNBC that the first-half revenue compared with just $1.16 billion in the first half of 2025, and asked whether it could grow to "keep pace with expectations."
"It is unclear how much it costs to generate each additional dollar of revenue as computing demand increases," she said.
But Anthropic's meteoric revenue growth slowed in the third quarter. It grew approximately 144% in the second quarter compared to the first quarter, followed by roughly 47% in the third quarter.
"What the prospectus didn't tell us is management's expectations around the sequential slowdown in the growth rate," said Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar.
"Substantially all of cost of revenue" is associated with compute and infrastructure costs, the filing states. It also says that operating margin and adjusted operating margin are expected to "fluctuate over time, particularly in periods when substantial incremental compute is delivered to us and we incur the associated expenses."
"Investors can see compute falling as a share of revenue, but not how much of the forward commitment is earmarked for training the next generation of models versus serving customers," Nick Patience, AI lead at the Futurum Group, told CNBC. "That split dictates future margins."
Questions also remain around whether compute costs can keep falling faster than commitments grow and if Anthropic can secure enough capacity to serve customers, he added.
Regarding demand across the AI and hyperscaler sector outstripping supply, the prospectus says that it had previously sought "quantities of compute from [cloud service providers] in excess of what those partners were willing to provide."
Later it says: "We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us."
Anthropic's structure as a public benefit corporation raises questions , too. Seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, have special voting power through a single Class F share equal to 50.1% of total voting power over matters brought to a shareholder vote.
Anthropic describes its capital and corporate governance structure as having "no direct public company precedent," in the filing.
"We also know now that management plans a series of different class share issues," said Morningstar's Field. "But what we don't know is whether investors will be fine with the lack of control implied, or will this impact the share price. Something we won't know until the shares start trading."
And finally the trillion-dollar question: the IPO valuation that Anthropic targets. The AI lab is keeping schtum about that, for now. It says simply it will be "determined by negotiations among us, the selling stockholders, and the representatives."
Given analyst estimates range between $1 trillion and $2 trillion, it will be a huge market event. If it's at the higher end of the range, it could bring back some of the swagger the AI sector has lost in recent weeks. If on the lower end, things could get ugly.
Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
SK Hynix's shares rose after the company reported record quarterly profit that sharply beat estimates, and announced over $25 billion in dividends and buybacks.
Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices said they will invest a total of $4 billion in Meta after the social media giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in AI infrastructure.
Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly AI infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power AI systems, Elon Musk said on Sunday.
Anthropic's S-1 was a trove of company intel, but one figure really caught my eye. The AI lab has more cash than almost every company in the U.S. And, as my colleague Leslie Picker writes, never before has a company gone public with anywhere near that much.

articles.title_orig: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times .
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia told the paper their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia and Megaspeed for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the paper: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed said its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: The Clever 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Feels Like An EV, But Never Needs Plugging In To Get 530 Miles Of Range
articles.title_zh: The Clever 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Feels Like An EV, But Never Needs Plugging In To Get 530 Miles Of Range
articles.content_orig:
For decades, car buyers in America have generally had access to four kinds of electrification. Most of the time, you can buy a battery electric car, a parallel hybrid car, a plug-in hybrid car, or, rarely, an extended-range electric car . In a weird, yet clever move, Nissan has gone a different direction. The 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid is an honest series hybrid, sort of like how a locomotive works. I got to drive it, and I feel like Nissan sort of created the best of both worlds in making a car that feels like an EV, but never needs to be plugged in.
For years, some car enthusiasts have considered Nissan to be a bottom-tier automaker of sorts. The poor reputation of early JATCO CVT-equipped Nissans arguably tarnished the brand’s reputation. It didn’t help when “ Big Altima Energy ” became an evergreen meme. Our comments still get populated with digs against Nissan CVTs.
Nissan has seemingly taken the criticism to heart, because from what I can see, the brand is going through a shocking turnaround on its product line. A couple of years ago, I found myself legitimately impressed with a rental-spec Rogue , and I’ve even found some joy in scooting around in base model Sentras, too.
But the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is on another level. I recently got to drive Nissan’s new moonshot in the mountains just outside of Santa Barbara, California, and my mind was blown by how much I enjoyed it. I’ll say it right now. If it were my own money, I’d buy a Rogue Hybrid over a Toyota RAV4 Hybrid. Yes, I said it.
( Full Disclosure : Nissan invited me out to Santa Barbara to try the new Rogue Hybrid. Nissan paid for my travel, an incredible stay at a Ritz-Carlton, and dishes of food so rich that I could barely pronounce their names.)
Engine : 1.5-liter ZR15DDTe fixed-compression turbocharged inline-three.
Transmission : Direct Drive.
Drive : Dual-motor all-wheel-drive.
Output : A generator making 146 horsepower and 171 lb-ft of torque, governed to 5,200 RPM. Plus a 202 horsepower front electric motor and a 134 horsepower rear motor. 225 horsepower combined system power.
Battery : 1.67 kWh lithium.
Fuel Economy : 41 MPG city, 36 MPG highway, 38 MPG combined.
Curb Weight : 4,107 pounds.
Base Price : $35,490 plus $1,595 destination fee.
Price As-Tested : $43,065 (SR Tech Package), before destination fee.
The Nissan Rogue Hybrid is a part of Nissan’s global strategy called Nissan Intelligent Mobility. Announced in 2016, Nissan Intelligent Mobility has become Nissan’s guiding vision for how to make its cars more convenient, greener, and more connected than before.
The biggest and most visible part of Nissan Intelligent Mobility is e-Power. Since 2016, Nissan has been developing a series hybrid technology that sets it apart from the competition.
In a typical hybrid car, a gasoline engine and an electric motor work in tandem to drive the vehicle. This is known as a parallel hybrid, and it’s the backbone for most hybrid cars. Some parallel hybrids don’t need to be plugged in, because the engine provides both locomotion and charging for the battery. Some parallel hybrids, known as plug-in hybrids, or PHEVs, have a sizable battery that gives the vehicle substantial all-electric range. When this range runs out, the engine kicks on, and driving then works similarly to how a regular parallel hybrid functions.
In a true series hybrid, the engine does none of the driving and cannot drive the wheels at all. Instead, all the engine does is act as a generator to provide electricity to an electric drive system. Today, series hybrids tend to be called extended-range EVs, and perhaps the most famous example is the BMW i3. The Chevrolet Volt is another great example, though its engine-generator can connect to the wheels in some situations.
Nissan admits that it doesn’t have the same brand image as its competitors in the hybrid space. Indeed, for many people, a Toyota is the default choice for a hybrid vehicle, and Toyota’s been churning them out for far longer than Nissan. Honda is probably the second choice for someone looking for a hybrid from a Japanese brand.
So, Nissan wanted to stand out in the crowd. It didn’t want to do the same thing as everyone else. Nissan also wanted to push the boundaries of what people expected from a hybrid. So, a decade ago, it went down the path of developing a series hybrid system.
Nissan says that the development of the original e-Power system was led by Naoki Nakada , who previously led the engineering behind the engine in the Nissan GT-R supercar. He was also the mind behind the original Nissan Leaf, and is on a mission to bring the GT-R experience to Nissan’s electrified lineup. Nissan continues with how he came up with the idea for e-Power:
The transition from traditional to fully electric mobility, however, won’t happen overnight. Some have hesitations toward EV ownership, such as driving range on a single charge, local and regional charging infrastructure, and cost. Realizing this, Nakada set out to ease customer concerns by developing an electrified powertrain that combines the thrilling performance of an electric motor with the ease of ownership a traditional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle offers. This is the origin of Nissan’s e-POWER technology.
Nissan e-POWER is different from typical hybrid systems as it simplifies the e-powertrain operation by having the high output electric motor solely provide power to the wheels. The lithium-ion battery powering the electric motor is recharged by a highly-efficient, on-board combustion engine acting as a power generator. For drivers, e-POWER offers a seamless and powerful acceleration experience similar to an EV, without the concern of a charging station. Instead, a visit to a gas station is all that’s needed to refuel. This makes electric mobility available to many more drivers than ever before.
Fuel efficiency is also at the core of Nissan’s e-POWER system with the engine operating at an optimized speed to recharge the battery. The engine is primarily activated at high cruising speeds or over rough road, when the sound of the engine can be masked by road noise. This ensures the driving experience is quiet like an EV in most driving scenes like a run around town.
Nissan’s e-Power system launched in Japan in 2016 in the Note city car, followed closely by the system getting fitted to the Serena minivan. Nissan’s tech has been a hit in Japan, and some 500,000 cars with an e-Power system were sold by 2021. Nissan e-Power cars are now sold in 68 countries, and Nissan says that it’s now made nearly two million of them.
But until now, no e-Power car has been sold in America. Nissan explains that the first two generations of e-Power were primarily developed for smaller vehicles and urban driving. It didn’t want to bring e-Power to America just yet because it knew that Americans liked bigger, faster cars, and wanted to feel comfortable driving them on the highway at high speeds.
Nissan has rectified that with the third-generation e-Power hybrid system. It’s designed to work specifically for larger cars and is engineered to gallop down an American superhighway. So, what car did Nissan put the new e-Power system into? Nissan selected its most popular vehicle in North America in one of its best-selling segments, the Rogue.
The Rogue enters an all-new generation in 2027, and at first, the new car will be hybrid-only. The pure internal combustion Rogue will continue on the old body for one more year before transitioning to the new body.
This new Rogue is going for a more dignified and upscale look than previous generations. Nissan says that this design is supposed to make the Rogue seem tough, refined, and fun all at the same time.
I really enjoy how much Nissan played around with hexagons. The grille and running lamps are hexagons, and I adore how both elements are blended together seamlessly. From a distance, it almost seems like the lights are emanating from the grille.

articles.title_orig: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.title_zh: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.content_orig:
IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates . Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
after newsletter promotion
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

articles.title_orig: Difficult negotiations lie ahead in Israel after Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority
articles.title_zh: Difficult negotiations lie ahead in Israel after Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority
articles.content_orig:
JERUSALEM — Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led , lie ahead.
The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.
“Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: “If you want to know if something’s happening behind the silence you’re hearing now, the answer is yes.”
The president will task someone with forming a government
Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?
Friday is when much of Israel starts winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them.
“There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.
The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.
If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.
Netanyahu and Likud target Arab parties without evidence
In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.
In Netanyahu’s first public comment Friday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties.
The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced results, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that “exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.
Opposition could assert control in the upcoming Knesset
Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021.
“I believe we should join forces and cooperate with the Arab parties, a legitimate population in the state of Israel,” said Miri Sklair, a resident of Jaffa.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into security failures before the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

articles.title_orig: Lenovo Googlebook 15 Review: Your Android Phone's New Best Friend
articles.title_zh: Lenovo Googlebook 15 Review: Your Android Phone's New Best Friend
articles.content_orig:
Googlebook's clumsy launch made me wish that I wasn't a product reviewer. I had to spend two weeks using a laptop with what felt like an unfinished operating system (cue the world's smallest violin), and throughout the entire process, I just kept thinking how nice it would be if Google had taken all of its biggest Googlebook features and slapped them on a mainline Linux distro instead of trying to reinvent the wheel.
Anyways, I tried to replicate these features on an old Surface Go that I bought for about $60 and loaded up with CachyOS, mainly because I thought it would be funny to do so, but also to demonstrate that you don't need to drop $800+ on a Googlebook to get some of its key functionality.
If you've never tried KDE Connect, go install it now. Not only does it enable texting from your Linux, Windows, or macOS desktop, but it lets you sync Android notifications to your PC, transfer files between your devices, and sync your clipboards. You can even use KDE Connect to control your PC from your phone , which feels like witchcraft, although it's arguably the least useful of these features.
Best of all, KDE Connect operates within your local Wi-Fi network, so it doesn't rely on external Google servers to sync your clipboard or notifications. You aren't restricted in which devices you connect, either. I've got several Android phones at my desk, plus an iPhone and Mac, and I can connect them all to my Linux laptop at once through KDE Connect if I want to.
GooglebookOS treats basic Android phone integration as a major selling point, which feels a bit odd to me, as KDE Connect and similar tools (including the official Microsoft Phone Link utility ) have been around for years. Plus, the Googlebook's Android integration is fairly broken at launch. I couldn't get basic features like Quick Share file transfers working at all when I reviewed the ASUS Googlebook 14 .
Though I will admit that the KDE Connect interface is kind of ugly. The good news is that Google Messages is available on the web, so I can just access it through my Linux laptop's browser if I want a prettier texting experience. There are also some file transfer tools with more attractive frontends than KDE Connect, such as Packet .
One of Googlebook's headline features—screen mirroring—didn't really work for myself, my colleagues, or too many other people at launch. It might still be kind of busted when this article goes live, for all I know.
Anyways, setting up Android phone mirroring in Linux took all but five minutes and worked without a hitch, all I had to do was install scrcpy , connect my Android phone to the laptop with a USB cable (after enabling USB debugging in Android's developer settings), and punch the scrcpy command into my terminal.
Not only does scrcpy mirror your Android phone's screen to your Linux desktop, but it lets you interact with the screen using your mouse and keyboard, just like how Googlebook phone mirroring is supposed to work. You can even use autoadb to automatically fire up scrcpy when you connect your phone to your PC, but I didn't bother, as I actually prefer the manual startup behavior.
To be honest, I was pretty delighted to see this working on my pathetic little Surface Go, which uses a Pentium 4415Y processor. But scrcpy's wireless mode, which you can trigger through the scrcpy --tcpip command (run the command while your phone is plugged in, then unplug it) didn't seem to be particularly fond of my Surface Go's Wi-Fi capabilities, and setting up wireless mirroring without a USB cable is somewhat cumbersome, so I guess scrcpy loses points there.
Is smartphone mirroring actually useful? To be perfectly honest, I haven't found any use for it beyond watching TikToks while reading emails on my Mac. But screen mirroring is a landmark Googlebook feature that didn't work for me or my colleagues at launch , so I had to replicate it in Linux out of spite.
Some of the Googlebook's Gemini integrations feel a bit lazy or clunky , but Magic Pointer is surprisingly polished. It's a desktop-based take on Android's "Circle to Search" feature: wiggle your cursor and highlight something on screen to show it to Gemini. The AI will explain what you're looking at or provide suggestions without pulling up a full chat window.
I managed to find some tools that loosely replicate Magic Pointer functionality. The best looking option is AIPointer , a tool that lets you select an area on your screen and send it to your LLM of choice. You can even use AIPointer to instantly send up to five files to an LLM, which sounds pretty handy to me.
The problem is that AIPointer and similar tools require an API key. And after spending a few weeks with a Googlebook, I've come to the conclusion that I don't use Magic Pointer enough to justify paying for it.
So, I've come up with a free solution—I can just take a screenshot and drag it into a ChatGPT or Claude window. If I need to ask an LLM about something on my screen, then it's probably going to require a conversation with some back-and-forth anyway, so it's not like I'm "wasting time" by opening a full chat.
This solution does lack some of Magic Pointer's automation features, such as the ability to add a date to your calendar by wiggling your cursor and pointing at it. But there are browser extensions like Text to Google Calendar that offer similar functionality, so I'm not too stressed about it.
Googlebook OS is built on Android's desktop interface, so naturally, it runs Android apps. It's a neat idea at a conceptual level, and it's something that's got a lot of potential if developers put their best foot forward, but it's pretty clunky at launch.
A lot of apps simply aren't available on the Googlebook Play Store, while others aren't optimized for the desktop at all. Plus, essential apps like Chrome currently lack key features that have been supported on Linux, Windows, and macOS for years.
Anyway, I tried replicating this functionality with Waydroid , which is a containerized utility that lets you run a full Android operating system on your PC. It even lets you go into multi-window mode so that each app is treated like a standalone window on your desktop.
But I quickly gave up on trying to replicate this Googlebook feature because it just isn't worth it on my poor, weak little Surface Go. There are visual bugs that I don't feel like putting in the effort to fix, and the performance is just generally rough. Nevermind the tedium of grabbing apps and setting up networking, which are just too time consuming, seeing as I'll probably never open Waydroid on my Surface Go again.
This is an area where the Googlebook obviously has a huge leg up. Whether Android apps are actually worth running on desktop is a matter of opinion, of course.
My favorite Googlebook feature, which is also available on Pixel 11, is the Rambler speech-to-text processor . I'll admit that this feature is somewhat niche, but it's the best speech-to-text tool I've used to date.
There are plenty of tools that accomplish Rambler-like functionality, most of which are based on OpenAI's Whisper model (which works offline and doesn't require API credits). Unfortunately, my poor Surface Go's Pentium 4415Y processor is way too weak for this level of realtime transcription. I gave the OpenWhispr and Handy frontends a go just to see what would happen, and my Surface Go threw up an overheating screen. Oops!
I can probably get around this issue by using a text-to-speech tool on my Android phone, copying the output to its clipboard, and syncing the clipboard to my Surface Go through KDE Connect. But there's not much utility in that outside of long-form writing since it's a bit tedious.

articles.title_orig: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.title_zh: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.content_orig:
The brutal business of selling mirrors is not for the faint-hearted. The challenge is category differentiation, given that a mirror has one simple task—reflection. One of Greg Jackson’s first jobs was working for a mirror manufacturer which, at best, broke even or made a small profit. And then he had an idea.
“We started making mirrors that had really wide frames,” the founder of Octopus Energy (the U.K.’s largest energy provider) told me. “And on a picture [on the internet], suddenly we had a mirror that looked different from everybody else’s. And they sold like hotcakes – and that transformed the business.”
Approaching a business from a different point of view is an essential ingredient in the hunt for innovation. Jackson’s essential insight when it came to mirrors was that, online, every product looked the same. That is what the customer saw. And he realized that if the customer saw something different (a mirror with a wide frame), they might buy it. Which they did.
Not seeing something that is obvious to an outsider is a firm’s “incumbency cost”— embedded in the regular behavior of doing the same thing tomorrow as you did yesterday. It is one of the most significant brakes on the ability to grow.
“I think the single biggest factor affecting Europe—and an issue the U.S. is not immune to—is incumbency,” he told me. “China and the Gulf are not held back by incumbent industries. Instead they are, at huge pace, delivering the new world. If I look at electric vehicles as an example, there’s not an incumbent car industry in China that’s struggling to manage the transition to an entirely new technology. But if I look at Europe, European governments and consumers want electric vehicles, but the European car companies have not yet been able to be competitive at building them.”
“If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need”
Chinese electric vehicle sales in Europe are growing rapidly. Chery has tripled sales in Europe in the past year, BYD has doubled, Geely is up a third, and SAIC is up 23%. Taking the four leading Chinese car makers together, their EV market share is now at 14.6%, up from 9.6%, according to the latest figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. In response to claims of state subsidized dumping by China, the European Union has applied duties of up to 35% on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Chinese cars are still over 20% cheaper to buy.
“Incumbents crowd out the innovators in many sectors and markets,” Jackson said. “It wasn’t the Post Office [the U.K.’s public mail service] that invented email. The music industry held back streaming and digital music for 10 to 20 years. What you need is routes to market for new technologies, and I think that can be a challenge in Europe because so many of the big industries essentially have a stranglehold on policy.
“Economists have said that nearly all productivity growth comes from new companies. If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need.”
Jackson said that Europe has a number of successful sectors that it can learn from—for example, the continent enjoys a vibrant and innovative fintech sector whereas in America “they take my card around the back of the bar because their terminals and processes are so dated.” Few people have seen a check in Europe in more than a decade.
Octopus grew out of the need for a new way to manage energy supply and demand. Jackson initially attempted to convince legacy businesses that they would be far more efficient with a fully overhauled technology platform but, after not progressing very far, decided that he could build a team that could modernize more quickly.
“The idea was that through technology, we would be able to provide lower costs because we’d be more operationally efficient,” he said. “We’d be more agile, so we can incorporate technologies like electric vehicles and solar panels and batteries directly into the energy system very efficiently. That would also help with cleaning up energy because you can use more renewables more cost-effectively if you’re more agile. We set out building that company in 2015, and nine years later, we became the biggest energy company in the UK, overtaking all the incumbents.
“We came from outside energy, we came from tech, and just like the people that built Uber didn’t come from personal transportation, and the people that built Airbnb didn’t come from hospitality, and the people that built Amazon didn’t own bookshops. What we were able to do is build an energy company not based around the assumptions of the industry, but using technology to meet the needs of customers.”
The brute force of market dynamics is pushing the world towards a different energy mix. In the European Union, wind and solar power produced more electricity than fossil fuels for the first time last year, according to Ember, the energy think tank.
“The technologies of electricity are improving exponentially, and the technologies of hydrocarbons are not,” Jackson said. “A car engine costs roughly the same now as it did 20 years ago. They’re not particularly more efficient. Meanwhile, an electric vehicle battery today costs 10 times less than it did 15 years ago. Solar panels cost 200 times less than they did 40 years ago. Wind turbines have come down two thirds in price over the last 20 years.”
Jackson was in China earlier in the year and said that electrification is continuing at pace, with battery swap stations, rather than recharging, reducing the amount of time drivers have to wait to between three and five minutes. “It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is. The drivers don’t care about the price of diesel.” Which might give Donald Trump pause for thought as he eyes both the American mid-term elections and the rising cost of fuel in the U.S.
Kamal Ahmed is the executive editorial director of Europe and the Middle East. Kamal is the author of Letter from London , Fortune Europe's weekly take on global business as seen from London. Previously, he was director of audio at The Telegraph and presenter of The Daily T podcast.

articles.title_orig: Beijing drills water cannons and drones near disputed South China Sea shoals
articles.title_zh: Beijing drills water cannons and drones near disputed South China Sea shoals
articles.content_orig:
Training off Second Thomas and Sabina shoals tests small boats, surveillance drones and simulated vessel boardings amid ongoing spats
China’s coastguard has carried out an exercise featuring water cannons and drones near two disputed reefs at the centre of its simmering South China Sea contention with the Philippines to prepare for “foreign infringement”, according to state media.
A China Coast Guard flotilla “recently” conducted “comprehensive maritime law-enforcement training” in the waters around Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal, according to state broadcaster CCTV, which did not specify dates.
The official television network stated that the drill had focused on foreign vessels “illegally” entering the waters around the two shoals, while covering surveillance, tracking, maritime traffic control and tactical manoeuvres by small boats.
It also included practising water cannon use, drone operations and optoelectronic evidence collection – a technique that uses optical and electronic sensors to detect and record evidence that may not be visible to the naked eye – according to the report.

articles.title_orig: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.title_zh: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.content_orig:
Novaya Gazeta , one of Russia’s last independent news outlets, announced on Friday it would close down operations due to pressure from authorities.
“Novaya Gazeta has been killed,” Editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement. “On November 9, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down our servers and leave…The Russian security services have forced the editorial team to cease operations.”
The newspaper, once edited by the Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov, has long been seen as a beacon of Russian investigative reporting.
Founded in the early 1990s partially under the patronage of former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya Gazeta had an adversarial relationship with the Kremlin, but had been under immense pressure from Russian authorities amid a widespread crackdown on the country’s media following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russian lawmakers criminalized the spread of “fake” news that discredits the Russian military in March 2022, forcing scores of journalists including those working at Novaya Gazeta to flee into exile. An offshoot publication, Novaya Gazeta Europe, is based in Riga, Latvia.
Sokolov told CNN he believes Novaya Gazeta’s fate reflected the situation in Russian society more broadly which faces a suppressed media landscape.
“The information space in Russia has disappeared,” Sokolov said. “People do not know, and have no way of finding out, even what is happening in the neighboring street, because the sources of news available to them are either stories about a Russia that does not exist or propaganda promoting the way of thinking the ruling elite wants to impose on the public.”
Novaya Gazeta initially suspended publication of its online and print editions in Russia following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, after receiving a warning from Russia’s media regulator, Roskomnadzor. The move came after Muratov took part, alongside other prominent independent Russian journalists, in an interview with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in March 2022.
Novaya Gazeta has a long history of investigating corruption and wrongdoing by various organs of the Russian state. Co-founder Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in October 2021 alongside Philippines journalist Maria Ressa for their “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression.”
In April 2022 , Muratov said he was attacked with acetone laced red paint while traveling on a train from Moscow to the city of Samara. The newspaper said in a statement that he nearly lost his sight, and the perpetrators were let go.
Six of the paper’s journalists have been murdered during its three and a half decades of operation, including Anna Politkovskaya, an ardent critic of President Vladimir Putin who reported extensively on human rights abuses in Chechnya. Politkovskaya was murdered outside her Moscow apartment in 2006, on Putin’s birthday.
Muratov and the newspaper itself were labeled “foreign agents.” Russian authorities have increasingly used the label as a way of casting aspersions on the credibility and independence of organizations and people carrying the designation. It’s a sign that the state sees them as associated with foreign influence and carries practical legal implications such as cumbersome financial penalties and reporting requirements.
“We carried on as long as we could, but we were evicted from our home and our donations platform that allowed us to receive financial support from our readers has been shut down,” Novaya Gazeta said in a statement published on Friday. “We have been stripped of all our resources. Entirely.”
Authorities revoked its license and blocked access to its website inside Russia. Oleg Roldugin, an investigative journalist for the paper was arrested earlier this year for “unlawful access to computerized information,” and the editor-in-chief Sokolov was detained for questioning and his home was searched in connection with the case.
In a statement to CNN the paper said, “we cannot continue working under the name ‘Novaya Gazeta.’ ‘Novaya’ no longer exists. One final issue will be published — and that’s it. After that, we’ll take a pause, reflect, and come up with a new life for ourselves.”
Muratov has remained a public voice campaigning for release of Russian political prisoners. The Atlantic in September reported on his efforts to lobby for US diplomacy to release jailed Russian dissidents. While critics say such efforts might potentially aid Putin’s bid for sanctions relief, the paper’s former editor and his international stature apparently could not shield the acclaimed newspaper from Russia’s machinery of repression.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s bloc loses parliamentary majority, Justice Department subpoenas California officials
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s bloc loses parliamentary majority, Justice Department subpoenas California officials
articles.content_orig:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.
Israel's final election count has confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has lost its parliamentary majority, but whether opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot can assemble a government to replace him remains an open question as negotiations begin behind closed doors.
The completed count, published early Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee , gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition alliance. The two predominantly Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats, placing them in a potentially decisive position.
Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest individual party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad with 12. Final voter turnout reached 77.9%, according to the Central Elections Committee results .
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot, right, and Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu are seen as election campaigns intensify two days before the vote as campaign posters of candidates are displayed on billboards and buildings across the streets ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for October 27, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
But the numbers leave neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority, opening a complex political struggle involving potential partnerships with Arab parties, ultra-Orthodox lawmakers or a unity government bringing together longtime rivals.
A source familiar with opposition discussions, who spoke to Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity, described the outcome as a "bitter stalemate," but not an impossible political situation.
The source said opposition leaders are approaching coalition negotiations with patience and experience rather than treating the inconclusive results as a defeat, arguing that the next government could depend on their ability to forge partnerships that previously seemed unlikely.
FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER
An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man holds his ballot as he votes in the parliamentary election at a polling station in Jerusalem on January 22, 2013. Israelis voted on Tuesday in an election widely expected to win Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a third term in office, pushing the Jewish State further to the right, away from peace with Palestinians and towards a showdown with Iran. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
In a potentially significant development Friday, Israeli journalist Yishai Cohen of Kikar HaShabbat reported that Rabbi Dov Lando, a leading ultra-Orthodox religious authority, had instructed lawmakers from Degel HaTorah, part of United Torah Judaism, to open discussions with the opposition.
According to the report, the objective is to reach an arrangement protecting the status of yeshiva students amid the longstanding dispute over mandatory military service.
Channel 12 reported that figures within the ultra-Orthodox party were considering allowing an Eisenkot-led minority government to survive through outside parliamentary support, potentially breaking with Netanyahu.
"Our votes are not in Netanyahu's pocket," party figures told Channel 12, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language report.
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher denied that any instruction to begin negotiations had been issued.
Such an arrangement would represent a significant shift from the party's longstanding alliance with Netanyahu. Eisenkot's pledge to expand military conscription among ultra-Orthodox men remains a major obstacle, although Channel 12 reported that party figures were willing to consider a compromise on the issue.
The source familiar with opposition discussions told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot's camp had been preparing for the possibility of cooperation with ultra-Orthodox parties well before the election, suggesting that some of the options now being discussed had already been under consideration behind the scenes.
According to the source, such an arrangement could require compromises over military service and potentially outside parliamentary support from Arab lawmakers, bringing together political factions whose positions appeared irreconcilable during the campaign.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, on October 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Another possibility rests with the Arab parties, which nearly doubled their parliamentary representation from 10 to 19 seats following a surge in turnout.
But the prospects of an Arab-backed government have drawn conflicting assessments.
Channel 12 reported Thursday that Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas had expressed deep skepticism about the possibility of establishing an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.
Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also argued that the available options had narrowed considerably, identifying a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or another election as the two principal remaining possibilities.
Mohammed Majadla, head of the news division at Radio Nas and a Channel 12 political commentator, offered a different assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital, arguing that both Ra'am and the Joint List were prepared to use their parliamentary influence to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.
"The two Arab lists agree on two things," Majadla said in the Hebrew-language interview. "First, they are prepared to do everything within the political process to ensure Netanyahu does not return to power."
According to Majadla, that could include joining a coalition, providing outside parliamentary support or abstaining from key votes.
He said their second shared priority was avoiding another election, which Arab political leaders fear could reverse their gains.
"The ball is now in Eisenkot's court, not in the Arab parties' court," Majadla said. "As far as the Arab parties are concerned, I can tell you they are truly prepared to do everything to make this happen."
Majadla suggested that public declarations should not necessarily be treated as final positions, particularly as parties seek leverage during coalition negotiations.
The difficulties extend beyond the Arab parties. Eisenkot's potential partners include politicians who strongly oppose cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, while several opposition leaders campaigned against relying on Arab lawmakers to govern.
NETANYAHU FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL FUTURE AS ISRAEL HEADS TO POLLS WITH IRAN THREAT LOOMING
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, of the Likud Party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Jack Guez / AFP via Getty Images)
A national unity government involving Likud and Yashar would offer a more straightforward mathematical route to a majority, but would require Eisenkot to reconsider his campaign pledge not to join a Netanyahu-led government.
For Netanyahu, the lengthy coalition formation process could provide additional opportunities. If Eisenkot receives the mandate to form a government but fails, President Isaac Herzog could assign the task to another candidate, potentially giving Netanyahu another chance to assemble a coalition. Strikes are planned across Italy on Friday, with widespread disruption expected as trade union Unione Sindacale di Base called on both public and private sector workers to strike, mobilise and protest, including at a major demonstration in Rome.
Renewed student protests are also expected to return to the street in major cities across Italy.
Meanwhile, the Cobas unions, together with Adl, Clap and Sial, have also called for a general strike across the public and private sectors, excluding transport.
The strike will also be a new test for public order, as students are set to return to the streets in all the main cities across Italy.
Friday's protests are directed against the rising cost of living, which unions say makes it increasingly difficult for people to cover essential expenses, as well as military spending.
Rail services are expected to be disrupted from 21:00 on Thursday until 20:59 on Friday, while the strike in air transport is expected to last for the entirety of Friday.
In local public transport, the impact will vary from city to city. The strike is also expected to affect taxi services throughout Friday, while motorway staff will begin their strike in the evening on Thursday.
Also on Friday, dock workers will mobilise globally against arms trafficking, rearmament policies and the militarisation of ports.
The action has been organised by several unions, including USB in Italy, the CGT in France and other trade union organisations in Greece, Turkey, Morocco and the Basque Country.
According to the organisers, workers from more than 100 ports in 17 countries and four continents have joined the mobilisation.
In Italy the protests will affect, among others, the ports of Genoa, Livorno, Trieste, Civitavecchia, Ancona, Ravenna and Gioia Tauro.
Among USB's key demands is for wages to rise in line with the cost of living, including through the reintroduction of the "scala mobile", a mechanism previously used to automatically adjust wages in line with inflation.
The union is also calling for measures to bring down the costs of essential goods, household bills and rents, and for a reduction in VAT on basic necessities.
According to USB, the government is allocating too many resources to military spending, while funding for health care, education and other public services remains inadequate.

articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.content_orig:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.
The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.
“ This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.
As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.
Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.
Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X .
Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.
The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.
Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .
David Ingram is a tech reporter for NBC News.

Four members of the same family were hurt early Thursday morning during a home invasion in Toronto’s affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood.
Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith told reporters police were called to the home on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:44 a.m. Oct. 29.
Three masked men allegedly forced their way into a home through the rear door and eventually confronted the family inside, Smith said. The men were armed with handguns, and one also had a hammer.
Four people were inside: a husband, his wife and their two adult children.
Global News has learned the two adult daughters are Maggie and Cristina Zohil-Morton. Their parents are listed on business profiles as David Morton and Doriana Zohil.
“A struggle ensued during this altercation in which the suspects fired their guns multiple times, and one victim was struck with a hammer,” Smith said.
“Three members of the family: the father and his two daughters, sustained gunshot wounds. Two victims remain in hospital with life-altering injuries, while the other two sustained non-life-threatening injuries.”
The suspects eventually fled in an SUV, but police did not have descriptions to provide.
Smith said a demand for valuables was made during the invasion, but investigators are not sure if the suspects escaped with anything as the family are not currently in the home.
“We have no information at this point to suspect that this particular home was targeted by the suspects. I’m not quite sure what their motives are at this time and whether or not they were in the area looking at other houses prior,” she said.
“People should be able to feel safe in their homes. I want to assure residents that the Toronto Police Service will do everything that we can to identify, locate, and bring these suspects to criminal justice.”
An investigation is underway.
Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

articles.title_orig: Putin shuts down Russia’s last independent newspaper
articles.title_zh: Putin shuts down Russia’s last independent newspaper
articles.content_orig:
Emily covers breaking news from all over the world. She previously reported on home news and politics for The Telegraph. You can reach her at emily.smith@telegraph.co.uk
Vladimir Putin has shut down Russia’s last independent newspaper.
The Russian president has ordered the closure of Novaya Gazeta after 33 years. It had previously been placed on a list of state enemies.
The newspaper, which is known for its critical coverage of Russian political and social affairs, has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow .
Sergei Sokolov, the paper’s editor-in-chief, said in a video statement on YouTube: “Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist. The Russian authorities, the Russian special services, have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
The paper was previously placed under investigation, with one of its journalists detained and the home of a senior editor searched.
Mr Sokolov added: “Novaya Gazeta has been killed... On Nov 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.
“They’re simply throwing us out, giving us barely any time to pack up. The Anna Politkovskaya museum is closing, and portraits of our friends who were killed are being taken down from the walls.”
Mr Sokolov was taken in for questioning earlier this month when his home was searched.
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993. It stopped publishing its print edition in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine.
A European edition of the paper – Novaya Gazeta Europe – was launched from Latvia to avoid censorship, but the website was later blocked by Russia.
Shortly after the invasion, Russia’s Basmanny Court also revoked Novaya Gazeta’s media licence.
Novaya Gazeta’s office, located on Potapovsky Lane, also housed a museum in tribute to Anna Politkovskaya, one of the newspaper’s reporters, who was killed 20 years ago this month when she was shot in front of her apartment in Moscow.
Dmitry Muratov, the newspaper’s former editor and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was travelling to Paris on Oct 19 for a commemoration of her death when he discovered the publication was being evicted.
He and Mr Sokolov gathered the paper’s remaining staff on Oct 26 in the basement of the building next door because it was too dangerous to talk in the office, owing to a break-in the previous night.
Staff agreed that it was time to shut down the publication.
“We haven’t died, they’ve killed us – along with the constitution,” Mr Muratov told The Economist. “You can only laugh at Article 29 of the constitution: ‘Censorship is prohibited’.”
He said Novaya Gazeta “was our city”, adding: “They’ve destroyed this city and we’re leaving. But we are not leaving our work.”
A change to the Russian Criminal Code was passed in March 2022, eight days after the invasion of Ukraine, which criminalised the dissemination of “false information” about the Russian military.
Since the law was passed, at least 30 independent Russian media outlets have been forced to close.
Oleg Roldugin, a Novaya Gazeta journalist, was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He pleaded not guilty, according to the state RIA news agency.

articles.title_orig: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.title_zh: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. articles.title_orig: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.title_zh: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen is done keeping its Chinese software locked inside China. The automaker said its China Electronic Architecture (CEA), built with local electric vehicle maker Xpeng , will underpin next-generation models bound for South America and South Africa. That marks a sharp break from the brand's old "in China, for China" approach.
Now that same software stack is being lined up for Europe. A report summarized by Reuters says Volkswagen is studying whether the China Electronic Architecture could form the basis for future mass-market cars from its VW, Skoda, and Cupra brands in Europe, with the plan still under discussion inside the group.
As reported by Reuters , Volkswagen plans to integrate China-developed technology into South American product lineups starting in 2030 . Volkswagen Group China now uses the China Electronic Architecture in five locally produced all-electric Volkswagen brand models, including the Yuzhong 06 and Yuzhong 07.
Volkswagen Group China laid out the broader package, called VEGA, at a Technology Day event in Hefei. VEGA ties together the China Main Platform, the China Electronic Architecture, and China-developed software and driver-assistance systems into one scalable package for software-defined vehicles across multiple segments.
The China Main Platform targets A-segment battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid models. Volkswagen's stated goal is more than 373 miles of CLTC range and roughly 11 kWh per 62 miles in its most efficient version. Volkswagen says the China-built software could extend further still, with the Europe proposal covering roughly three quarters of the next-generation lineups for VW, Skoda, and Cupra .
Exports of China-developed vehicles are also starting to ramp up around 2026. China-built Volkswagens are already heading to markets such as Mexico and parts of Southeast and Central Asia, with more destinations planned afterward. That export push would run alongside the deeper platform integration planned for 2030.
The architecture trims the number of electronic control units by about 30 percent compared with Volkswagen's older setups. Volkswagen says that reduction is central to cutting development costs and complexity across its lineup.
It's a hardware play as much as a software one. Volkswagen intends to bring the same architecture to plug-in-hybrid and combustion models in China by 2027, which would widen its reach past the battery-electric vehicles where it currently lives and give future gas and hybrid products the same software backbone.
Looking further out, Volkswagen is targeting Level 4 automated driving by 2029, built on a third-generation version of the China Electronic Architecture paired with a Volkswagen-developed C7H control chip. That automated-driving target sits alongside the South America plan and the potential European rollout.
The strategy also threatens to sideline Rivian , Volkswagen's US software partner in a $5.8 billion investment central to CEO Oliver Blume's technology plans. A separate report from German outlet Manager Magazin said core brand chief Thomas Schäfer is weighing a proposal to use China-developed software as the basis for future Volkswagen, Skoda, and Cupra models, which would leave Rivian focused on other group brands even if the joint venture itself stays in place.
